analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC police telecom and cable companies for unfair or deceptive practices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote — it died in the Energy and Commerce Committee at the end of the 114th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal consumer-protection law has long carved out one group of companies: 'common carriers' — phone, wireless, and broadband providers regulated under communications law. This bill would have removed that carve-out by narrowing the statutes that trigger it, letting the Federal Trade Commission bring unfair-or-deceptive-practices cases against telecom and cable companies just as it can against other businesses. The bill was introduced, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of phone, wireless, broadband, and cable service. Today the FTC cannot bring unfair-or-deceptive-practices cases against these carriers because the Federal Trade Commission Act exempts common carriers subject to the Communications Act [S2][S3]. The bill narrows the definition of 'Acts to regulate commerce' so the Communications Act no longer triggers that exemption, closing the gap [S3]. That would give the FTC power to act on hidden fees, misleading billing, and deceptive claims by carriers [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The Federal Trade Commission Act exempts common carriers from FTC enforcement; the bill amends the definition of 'Acts to regulate commerce' so the Communications Act of 1934 no longer counts, removing telecom carriers' exemption [S3].

The bill would authorize the FTC to enforce the FTC Act against common carriers subject to the Communications Act, bringing telephone and wireless companies under the same consumer-protection enforcement that applies to other businesses [S2].

The FTC enforces a general prohibition on unfair and deceptive acts in commerce; extending it to carriers would let the agency pursue practices like undisclosed fees or misleading service claims across the telecom sector, which a single-industry regulator may not reach the same way.

analysis.who_pays: Telephone, wireless, broadband, and cable companies, which would face FTC investigations and enforcement actions and new legal exposure for their billing and marketing practices. Consumers could indirectly bear some compliance costs passed through in prices.

drawbacks.text: Jurisdiction overlap: carriers are already regulated by the Federal Communications Commission under communications law, so FTC enforcement could produce overlapping or conflicting rules; carriers argue sector-specific oversight is better suited to their industry than general consumer-protection law.
Compliance and litigation costs for carriers would rise, and some of that cost is likely to show up in consumer prices — a trade-off a supporter would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: telecom and cable companies are among the most complained-about consumer businesses, and giving the FTC general deceptive-practices authority over them closes a long-standing enforcement gap. The main costs are regulatory duplication with the FCC and some pass-through of compliance costs. The overlap is manageable and the benefit to consumers of transparency in fees and marketing outweighs it, though the bill's one-paragraph text left the mechanics of the FCC–FTC split to be worked out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and ended without a hearing, markup, or vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry McNerney introduced the bill on May 13, 2016, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
One week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, where it stayed; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill drew zero cosponsors [S4], and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 without the bill receiving any vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telephone, wireless, broadband, and cable companies are better off: they keep the FTC exemption that shields them from general unfair-and-deceptive-practices enforcement, with no need to argue against the bill on the floor because it never got that far.

for.name: Rep. Jerry McNerney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; recruited no cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; sent it to subcommittee where it ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one spoke against the bill in the record, so the partisan shape is unknowable; a lone Democrat sponsored it and it drew no cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.industry: Telephone, wireless, broadband, and cable carriers
industries.note: These companies are currently exempt from the FTC Act as common carriers subject to the Communications Act; the bill would strip that exemption and expose them to FTC deceptive-practices enforcement [S2][S3]. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against consumers, who have no general federal deceptive-practices remedy against them today.
The FTC's jurisdiction would expand to cover telecom carriers, aligning the enforcer's reach with consumer interests [S2].
